awd_titl_txt: ERI: Progressive Formation and Collapse Mechanisms of Sinkholes Caused by Defective Buried Pipes
awd_abstract_narration:
This Engineering Research Initiation (ERI) award supports research that aims to understand why and how sinkholes form above defective buried pipes. Sinkholes induced by defective buried pipes have become a substantial threat to community safety, resulting in fatalities, damage to buildings and infrastructure, and economic loss. However, the collapse mechanism of sinkholes above buried pipes remains unclear, making prediction of sinkhole collapses difficult. In this project, the research team will identify the most susceptible soil and water flow conditions around  defective pipes leading to sinkhole initiation and develop models to predict their growth. Currently, the US has more than one million miles of pipes nearing the end of their service lives that pose a sinkhole risk to their communities. This project will expand our understanding of  formation and collapse mechanisms of such sinkholes to provide predictive capabilities. The research will also be complemented by establishing a responsive and flexible educational and outreach program based on curriculum development and K-12 summer camps that can motivate young students to pursue their college education in STEM fields.

The research goal of this project is to predict sinkholes caused by defective buried pipes based on understanding of progressive formation and collapse mechanisms. To achieve this goal, the objectives are to (i) identify critical hydrogeological parameters leading to initiation of soil internal erosion around defective pipes through soil erosion tests in the laboratory; (ii) model the time-dependent progressive evolution of sinkholes induced by defective buried pipes using a sinkhole simulator; and (iii) develop an analytical method to predict the collapse timing and size of sinkholes considering external loads based on time-dependent soil arching models. This project will test three hypotheses: (1) internal soil erosion around defective buried pipes initiates when the ratio of hole diameter to D85 (i.e., 85% percent fines) of soil infill surrounding the pipe reaches a threshold value related to the hydraulic gradient; (2) sinkholes in a submerged zone will be cone-shaped with an angle from the horizontal direction that equals to the surrounding soil friction angle; and 3) sinkholes above the submerged zone will be dome-shaped, and collapse of the dome will be exaggerated by external loads. This project will allow the PI to advance  knowledge of the sinkhole formation and collapse around defective buried pipes and to lay a firm foundation for his long-term career focused on safety and sustainability of buried civil infrastructures.

This award reflects NSF's statutory mission and has been deemed worthy of support through evaluation using the Foundation's intellectual merit and broader impacts review criteria.

por.por_cntn:
Sinkholes can develop beneath roads when defective, deteriorated, or leaking underground pipes allow water to erode and transport surrounding soil. The resulting underground cavities can remain hidden until they cause pavement settlement, cracking, or sudden collapse, posing significant safety risks and causing costly transportation disruptions. The scale of the aging pipeline problem in the United States is substantial, with approximately 2.2 million miles of buried pipelines approaching or exceeding their service life. In addition, approximately 240,000 water-main breaks occur annually in the United States, highlighting the widespread potential for pipe-related soil erosion and ground instability. Water leaking from a defective pipe can progressively erode the surrounding soil and form a hidden cavity beneath a roadway long before a visible sinkhole develops. Before this project, however, there was no established method for predicting the timing, extent, and progression of sinkhole collapse caused by defective pipes, limiting the ability of goverment agencies to proactively prevent and mitigate these failures.

The major contributions of this project include: (1) development of an experimental apparatus to quantify soil loss around defective pipes and identify the critical hydrogeological conditions that initiate and control soil erosion as shown in Figure 1; (2) development of an analytical method to predict the propagation of ground settlement to the surface while accounting for soil stiffness; and (3) development of methods to predict sinkhole collapse timing and spatial extent based on large-scale sinkhole simulation tests (Figure 2) and numerical modeling. The key factors governing the sudden collapse of pipe-induced sinkholes were also identified.

The project advanced fundamental knowledge of pipe-induced sinkhole formation in three important areas: (1) the critical hydrogeological conditions that initiate soil loss caused by pipe leaks; (2) the progressive development and growth of underground cavities; and (3) the mechanisms governing sinkhole collapse. The research resulted in 12 journal articles, two master's theses, and one conference paper, which have been published or are currently under review.

The project also provided significant educational and workforce-development opportunities. One postdoctoral researcher, one Ph.D. student, two master's students, and four undergraduate students received training in experimental geotechnical engineering, numerical modeling, data analysis, and sinkhole mechanics. More than 300 K-12 students were engaged through educational activities demonstrating sinkhole formation and its underlying mechanisms, helping to increase awareness of geotechnical engineering and encourage interest in STEM fields. Short courses and invited lectures were also provided to professionals and researchers to disseminate the project findings. These activities helped translate the research outcomes into improved understanding and practical approaches for the prevention, early detection, and mitigation of sinkholes caused by defective underground pipes.
